text.tspan: 02 · POST /v1/route — how a request becomes a governed decision
Conclusion: the caller never names a model, and governance policy runs BEFORE cost and complexity selection — so a cost optimisation can never reach a model policy has not approved.
Caller · lane service or webui

"costCeilingUsd": 0.25,

PRINCIPLE IV — what is NOT in this request
There is no "model" field.
There is no "vendor" field.
There is no "deployment" field.
And there will not be one: a field that exists is a field that
eventually gets used. dataClassification states what the data IS;
it is not a routing preference. Omitting it is a 400, never an
assumption of "Public".
THE ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING
catalog → PolicyGate.Evaluate() → eligible → TierSelector.Select()
Policy decides what is PERMISSIBLE.
The router then decides what is APPROPRIATE among the permissible.
Reverse these two and a cost optimisation can reach a model
governance has not approved. The order is asserted by test, not
left to code reading.
Beat 5 — the swap nobody deployed for
An approver toggles Anthropic off on /policy. No redeploy, no code
change, no prompt change. The identical request replans across the
remaining approved vendors and the exclusion reason reads:
"Vendor Anthropic is not approved under policy set
'CapitalMarkets-US'."
Set dataClassification to Restricted and every hosted vendor is
excluded; execution lands on the open-weight model on managed
compute inside the VNet.
router-service · POST /v1/route
Internal Container Apps ingress. There is no public FQDN.
Rejects a caller without the Router.Invoke app role with 403.
RoutingPlanner.Plan() is the single entry point and the one place
the evaluation order is decided — calling TierSelector directly
would bypass the gate.
ComplexityScorer.Score(hints)
Pure, deterministic, caller-supplied signals only — never inferred from model output.
tokens/32000 × 0.40 + multiStep × 0.25 + retrieval × 0.20 + toolCalls × 0.15
Rounded to 4dp, clamped 0–1. IndicatedTier: <0.35 Economy · <0.70 Standard · else Premium.
STEP 1 — PolicyGate.Evaluate(catalog, policySet, classification, region)
Runs FIRST, against the full multi-vendor catalog. Excludes, in order:
· region not in policy.AllowedRegions → the whole catalog is excluded
· vendor not in policy.ApprovedVendors
· classification > policy.MaxClassification[vendor]
· cost > policy.MaxCostPerRequestUsd
Every exclusion carries prose fit to read aloud to a governance audience.
STEP 2 — TierSelector.Select(score, ceiling, eligible)
Sees ONLY the policy-eligible candidates. Prefers the indicated tier; if it is
unaffordable or unavailable it takes the most capable tier that is both.
The ceiling is a control, not a report.
Vendor invocation
The selected deployment is invoked over the Foundry private endpoint.
APIM metering / content safety is specified but not yet in Terraform.
No silent retry on a different tier — that would corrupt the cost figures.
FOUR OUTCOMES — three of them are HTTP 200
A governed "no" is a correct answer, not an error.
RefusedByPolicy → HTTP 200
Policy left no eligible candidate. selectedDeployment is null and every
candidate is listed with its reason.
Returned as 200 on purpose: a refusal is a correct, governed outcome.
Modelling it as 4xx would invite retry-on-error, and the one thing that
must never happen is a retry that finds an unapproved model.
Denied → HTTP 402
Cost ceiling. Even the cheapest available tier projects above the ceiling.
"Cheapest available tier Economy projects 0.310 USD against a ceiling
of 0.250 USD."
Kept distinct from RefusedByPolicy: "too expensive" and "not permitted"
are different conversations with different people.
Downgraded → HTTP 200
Complexity indicated a higher tier; the ceiling did not allow it.
Routed to the most capable affordable tier, with the downgrade named
in the rationale. This is wow moment B on the comparison screen.
Routed → HTTP 200
Routed to the tier the complexity score indicated, within both the policy
ceiling and the request ceiling. Rationale names the deciding factor in a
plain sentence, because the presenter reads it aloud on stage.
EVERY outcome above — including both refusals — is persisted and audited
A denial is never silently absorbed; it is always surfaced to the UI. Principle VI: one correlationId spans the whole lifecycle.
Cosmos · routerDecisions
Partitioned by /correlationId.
Inputs, candidate tiers with per-candidate rejection
reasons, policy exclusions, outcome, rationale,
policySetId and policySetVersion.
GET /v1/decisions/{correlationId} (Router.Read).
Cosmos · auditEvents (append-only)
Every step writes one record keyed by the same correlationId.
Append-only and retained for the life of the environment.
AC-8: the whole chain is reconstructable in ONE query —
which is exactly what Beat 8 does from an unrehearsed pick.
Scoreboard · Application Insights (Cosmos change feed as fallback)
GET /v1/scoreboard?window=15m — count, total cost, baseline cost,
savings delta, p50/p95 latency, tier distribution, mean quality by lane.
Visible within 5 seconds (AC-5). Sampling is disabled for router and
approval telemetry; the UI labels the degraded source when it falls back.

Legend — what the colours mean
Governed chokepoint / deterministic code the exchange depends on.
Governance gate. Runs before any cost reasoning.
Public or refusal / denial. The single public surface, or a governed "no".
Cost control acting — a downgrade, visible and explained.
Inside the VNet / private endpoint only. No public data-plane endpoint.
The test of Principle IV, stated as an experiment
Two requests with byte-identical bodies, submitted under different policy sets, may execute on different vendors and both succeed.
If swapping a vendor requires a code change, a redeploy, or a prompt edit, the principle is violated — no matter what the diagram says.
The router is deterministic code and always will be: routing the thing that decides routing would be circular, and a compliance audience
will read this assembly line by line. It is under a 70% coverage gate for exactly that reason.
